lesson.title: Economic Developments and Innovations in the Industrial Age
lesson.summary: How laissez-faire ideas, limited liability, stock markets, and transnational businesses changed economies.
learningGoals: Explain the development of economic systems, ideologies, and institutions.
Explain how new financial institutions supported industrial growth.
lesson.bigIdea: New economic ideas and institutions, from Adam Smith's free-market arguments to limited liability and global banks, supported industrial capitalism.
lesson.context: Mercantilism dominated European economic thinking before 1750. Industrialization encouraged new arguments for free markets and new ways to raise capital.

sections.title: Laissez-faire ideas

blocks.text: Adam Smith argued in 1776 that the division of labor and free markets would increase wealth. Laissez-faire capitalism held that government should interfere little in the economy.
Critics pointed to monopolies, harsh working conditions, and economic crises, and some called for regulation.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Laissez-faire was an argument, not a description of reality. Governments still passed tariffs, built railroads, and regulated some industries.

sections.takeaway: Free-market ideas challenged mercantilism and shaped industrial economies.

sections.title: New financial institutions

blocks.text: Limited liability, introduced in Britain in 1855, meant investors could lose only what they had invested. Stock exchanges grew as more people bought shares.
Banks and businesses operated across borders. The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, founded in 1865, financed trade across Asia.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Limited liability lowered investors' risk, which drew more capital into companies and allowed larger enterprises.

sections.takeaway: New financial tools mobilized capital for large industrial firms.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that government should interfere as little as possible in the economy.
A legal rule that investors can lose only the money they put into a company, not their other property.
Splitting production into many small tasks, each done by a different worker, to increase output.

connections.title: From joint-stock companies to stock markets
connections.body: Unit 4 described joint-stock companies such as the VOC. Limited liability and stock exchanges expanded the practice of selling shares.
connections.transferQuestion: How did limited liability build on the joint-stock model?
connections.feedback: Compare how each spread risk among investors.
